events.subtitle: Revived Quintessence — all-new repertoire premiere

priority_review.rationale: This is not a routine festival set. Rosewoman is reviving Quintessence, an ensemble she launched in 1986, reuniting veteran members including Greg Osby and Tyshawn Sorey while premiering an all-new repertoire of recent compositions ahead of a planned 2026 recording. The combination of lineage, new work and deep ensemble language clears the S threshold for a protected DMV date.

en.why_it_matters: This is exactly the kind of festival booking that becomes more interesting the closer you look. Rosewoman is not dusting off an old band for nostalgia: she is reopening Quintessence with veteran voices from its history, including Greg Osby and Tyshawn Sorey, and using that lineage to premiere an entirely new body of recent compositions. That makes the set about continuity and invention at the same time — a living ensemble language being reactivated, not reconstructed.
en.trip_verdict: S. Protect the afternoon in DC. It stays below S+ because it is part of a broader festival/presentation series rather than a singular farewell or one-night historical reunion.

events.subtitle: Randy Weston Centennial

priority_review.rationale: The centennial is being carried by direct members of Randy Weston's African Rhythms ensembles rather than by an unrelated tribute band: T.K. Blue, Neil Clarke, Alex Blake and Frank Lacy, joined by Weston acolyte Sharp Radway. That direct lineage, in the 100th-birthday year, makes the set historically and musically specific enough for S.

en.why_it_matters: The important word here is alumni. This is not a centennial program assembled by musicians who merely admire Randy Weston: T.K. Blue, Neil Clarke, Alex Blake and Frank Lacy came through his African Rhythms bands, with Sharp Radway carrying the language as an acolyte. Weston's music made African rhythm, blues, large-form composition and improvisation part of one continuous vocabulary; hearing that vocabulary carried by musicians who lived inside it gives the centennial real lineage rather than tribute-band distance.
en.trip_verdict: S. Protect this DC JazzFest set and build the festival day around it if Randy Weston's African Rhythms language matters to you. It justifies a dedicated DMV outing and a reasonable regional drive; it remains below S+ because it is a centennial tribute by alumni rather than a unique surviving reunion with Weston himself.
